When a case is rendered via the REST API or browser views, all connector instances associated with that case were included in the response regardless of the requesting user's permissions.

This means that any authenticated user with read access to a case could observe connector metadata belonging to other users (personal-scope connectors) or other organizations (org-scope connectors), including connector URLs, descriptions, UUIDs, and potentially embedded API credentials.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user account with at least read access to the affected case
- The case must have connector instances attached that belong to other users or organizations

Impact:
- Disclosure of personal connector endpoints and credentials of other users
- Disclosure of organization-scoped connector metadata across organizational boundaries
- Enumeration of connector infrastructure (URLs, UUIDs, descriptions) not intended for the viewer

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its task management workflow. When a user reopens a completed task (by toggling its completion state or changing its status to a non-finished value) or creates a new task within a completed privileged case, the parent case is automatically revived (un-completed, status reset to Created, finish date cleared). The system failed to enforce the required Admin or Case Admin privilege check before performing this case revival side effect.

A user with basic task-level permissions (e.g., editor, queuer, or queue admin) could trigger the revival of a completed privileged case through the browser interface or the REST API, without holding the elevated role required for case-level operations. This could disrupt case lifecycle management, clear completion metadata, and potentially expose the case to further unauthorized modifications.

The vulnerability affects both the browser-based task completion/status-change endpoints and the corresponding API endpoints, as well as the task creation flow.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel contains an authorization bypass in the browser-based admin user editing interface. The edit_user view in the admin panel verified that a non-platform-admin user could only edit accounts belonging to their own organization, but it did not verify that the target account was not a platform-admin account. As a result, an authenticated user holding an organization-admin role could open the edit form for any platform-admin account and submit modifications, including changes to credentials, roles, or other account attributes.

The API layer already enforced a restriction preventing non-admin users from targeting admin accounts, but the browser-based admin view lacked the equivalent check, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary.

Impact:
- Unauthorized modification of platform-admin account data (integrity)
- Potential lockout or privilege manipulation of platform administrators (availability)
- Escalation of an organization-admin role to effectively control platform-level administration

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its user deletion functionality. Organization-scoped administrators (org admins) are able to delete platform-level administrator accounts through both the browser-based admin interface and the REST API.

The existing authorization logic verified that an org admin could only target users within their own organization, but it did not enforce the privilege hierarchy between organization admins and platform admins. As a result, an authenticated org admin could issue a deletion request against any platform-admin account belonging to the same organization, causing the target account, its sessions, and related records to be permanently removed.

Impact:
- Loss of platform-level administrative oversight
- Potential disruption of platform-wide management functions
- Removal of higher-privilege accounts that should be protected from lower-privilege roles

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0

A vulnerability exists in the flowintel application's calendar functionality that allows unauthorized access to private case data. The task calendar queries failed to enforce visibility checks on the parent case associated with tasks. Specifically, tasks assigned to a user or belonging to the user's organization were returned in calendar views (including browser and API ICS feeds) without verifying whether the user had permission to view the parent case. This allowed users to potentially discover and access details of private cases they were not authorized to view, leading to information disclosure.

The issue affected the default task visibility logic and the assigned-only task queries. The fix ensures that case visibility is rechecked in addition to task assignment or organization membership, preventing the exposure of private case data in calendar outputs.

Affected versions: flowintel < 4.1.0

flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its recurring reminder notification subsystem. When a user is subscribed to recurring notifications for a case, the system does not re-verify the recipient's current access rights to that case before generating or displaying the notification.

As a result, a user who previously had access to a private case and later had that access revoked can still:
- Receive recurring reminder notifications containing case-related content.
- View stored reminder notifications in their notification list, including notification counts, even though they no longer have permission to view the underlying case.

The vulnerability affects both the notification creation path (recurring reminder generation) and the notification display path (listing and counting stored reminders). The issue arises because the authorization check performed at subscription time is not re-applied at delivery or retrieval time.

Security impact is limited to information disclosure: an unauthorized user may observe case titles, reminder messages, and associated metadata that they no longer have permission to access. No integrity or availability impact is indicated by the patch.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

FlowIntel's alerting module contained an authorization bypass in the alert access control logic. When an alert was linked to a private case, the system relied solely on connector ownership (user or organization) to determine access, without verifying that the requesting user still held valid membership in the associated private case.

This meant that a user who was a connector owner of an alert could continue to read alert details, review history, raw payloads, and action comments, and could perform review-status updates or case-creation actions, even after their access to the linked private case had been revoked or they were never a member of that case.

Additionally, a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap existed: after a review-status update or a competing case-creation claim was committed, the response could disclose private case identifiers or review history to a user whose access had been concurrently removed by another session linking the alert to a private case.

Impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of private case data (review comments, raw payloads, action history) through alert endpoints.
- Unauthorized modification of alert review status and creation of cases from alerts the user should no longer access.
- Leakage of a competing case identifier to an unauthorized user during concurrent case-creation races.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel is a case management application that enforces an approval workflow for tasks in privileged cases. Tasks in such cases are required to start in a Requested status, meaning they must receive explicit approval before becoming active.

A logic flaw in the task-creation path allowed tasks to be initialized with a Created status (bypassing the approval step) in two scenarios:

- When a task was created from a template and no acting user was supplied, the privileged-case check was skipped entirely, leaving the task in Created status.
- When a case was created from a template, all copied tasks were unconditionally assigned the Created status regardless of the case's privileged designation.

An authenticated user with the ability to create tasks from templates or to instantiate cases from templates could therefore place tasks directly into an active state within privileged cases, circumventing the intended approval gate. This may expose restricted case content or permit actions that should require supervisory sign-off.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

FlowIntel's chatbot component used a single shared MCP (Model Context Protocol) session and process-wide environment variable to pass per-user API credentials to a child process. Because the session and the ambient FLOWINTEL_API_KEY environment variable were shared across all concurrent requests, a user's authenticated identity could be applied to another user's tool invocation, or a stale/ambient credential could be inherited by a new request.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to the chatbot interface.
- Concurrent or overlapping chatbot tool invocations from different users, or a request made after another user's credentials were written to the process environment.

Impact:
- A lower-privilege user could read data belonging to a higher-privilege user (e.g., private investigation cases).
- A user whose session was invalidated (deleted, password changed, key revoked) could still operate under a previously cached ambient credential.
- The parent process environment was mutated with user-specific secrets, creating a persistent credential leak surface.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel contains a vulnerability in the case and task classification usage endpoints that allows authenticated users to view classification data associated with cases they do not have permission to access.

The affected endpoints, which provide lists of used taxonomies, tags, galaxies, clusters, and custom tags, did not properly enforce object-level access controls. While the endpoints required authentication, they failed to filter the returned data based on the requesting user's visibility permissions for the underlying cases. This allowed any authenticated user to enumerate classification usage across all cases, including private or restricted cases belonging to other organizations or users.

This issue could lead to the disclosure of sensitive information, such as the existence of specific cases, the types of threats or indicators associated with them, and the relationships between different classification elements, potentially aiding an attacker in reconnaissance or targeting.

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

flowintel contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case history feature. When a user views the history of a case they are authorized to access, the history output includes references to other cases (linked, unlinked, or forked) without verifying whether the requesting user has permission to view those referenced cases. This exposes the identifiers and titles of cases that the user should not be able to discover.

The vulnerability affects multiple output paths:
- Browser-based case history view
- API history endpoint
- Plain-text history download
- Markdown history download
- Report timeline generation

An authenticated user with access to any single case can enumerate the existence and identifiers of other cases by reading the history of a case they can access. This bypasses the intended per-case access control model and may reveal the existence of sensitive investigations, their identifiers, and associated metadata to unauthorized users.

The raw audit storage is not modified; the issue is solely in the presentation layer failing to filter references to inaccessible cases before returning history data to the user.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

memtomem-stm is a short-term memory proxy gateway with proactive memory surfacing for AI agents. From 0.1.0 until 0.1.34, untrusted long-term and working-memory fields can introduce Markdown or HTML-compatible structure into the surfaced-memory envelope because those fields are not serialized as inert data. A crafted memory can create misleading structural boundaries or visually conceal surfaced content, affecting how a consuming agent interprets the memory context. Ordinary natural-language persuasion remains a residual model-level risk and is outside the structural serialization flaw. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.34.

Netatalk is a Free and Open Source file server suite for Unix-like operating systems. From 3.1.0 until 4.5.1, the afpd Spotlight RPC fetchQueryResultsForContext: reply path in etc/afpd/spotlight_marshalling.c calls the top-level sl_pack function from sl_pack_filemeta on a shifted sub-buffer without passing the remaining capacity of the outer DSI reply buffer. An authenticated AFP client can request an amplified nested file-metadata tree so the nested packer applies MAX_SLQ_DAT relative to the shifted pointer and writes beyond struct DSI::data. The out-of-bounds write corrupts heap memory beyond the DSI reply buffer. This issue is fixed in version 4.5.1.

MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. Prior to 8.6.5, an unauthenticated reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in OGC API Features collection-items HTML output allows crafted offset or limit query parameter values from raw CGI request handling in src/mapogcapi.cpp to reach template.params.offset or template.params.limit. share/ogcapi/templates/html-bootstrap/collection-items.html inserts those values without quoting or escaping into a script element. A victim who follows a crafted request can have the script element terminated by attacker-controlled markup, causing arbitrary JavaScript to execute under the MapServer origin and enabling access to browser-session data, actions as the victim, and content manipulation. This issue is fixed in 8.6.5.

MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. Prior to 8.6.5, MapServer's MySQL JOIN implementation in src/mapjoin.c copies the source layer attribute selected by JOIN ... FROM into joininfo->target and inserts it into the query built by msMySQLJoinNext() without parameterization or SQL escaping. When MySQL JOIN support is enabled, an attacker who can control that source feature attribute, including through imported shapefile or DBF data or another untrusted spatial source, can inject SQL operators or expressions that change the intended JOIN predicate. This can bypass the intended key comparison and expose unrelated records from the MySQL or MariaDB JOIN table through output templates, query responses, or downstream application logic. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. Prior to 8.6.5, MapServer's PostgreSQL JOIN implementation in src/mappostgresql.c copies the source layer attribute selected by JOIN FROM into joininfo->from_value and embeds it without parameterization or escaping into a dynamically generated PostgreSQL query executed by PQexec(). When PostgreSQL JOIN support is enabled, an attacker who can control that source feature attribute can inject quote characters and SQL operators that alter the intended WHERE predicate. This second-order injection can cause unintended rows and JOIN attributes to be returned, potentially exposing information from unrelated PostgreSQL records. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

Pozeiden is a MermaidJS renderer written in Zig. Prior to 0.3.0, Pozeiden emits attacker-controlled Mermaid values into SVG attributes or markup without sufficient XML escaping or URL scheme validation, and first-party consumers such as zigmark and policypress embed the generated SVG raw into HTML. The click href syntax can introduce a dangerous URL scheme or break out of an attribute; style, classDef, ::: class assignment, and linkStyle color values can inject fill or stroke markup; color and font-weight values can escape text attributes; %%{init}%% themeVariables can inject global renderer attributes; and quadrant y-axis labels can introduce raw markup. These paths involve src/svg/writer.zig, src/renderers/flowchart.zig, src/renderers/quadrant.zig, and src/root.zig. An attacker who can influence rendered Mermaid source can therefore store script-bearing SVG that executes when another user views the published HTML. This issue is fixed in version 0.3.0.

mcp-ssh-manager is an MCP server for managing servers over SSH with human approval, an encrypted vault, and a live audit trail. Prior to 3.6.7, ssh_db_list, ssh_db_dump, ssh_db_import, and ssh_db_restore in src/database-manager.js interpolate caller-controlled database, table, collection, file path, user, host, port, and password values into shell-evaluated command strings without neutralization. Shell metacharacters in these arguments therefore execute arbitrary commands on the configured SSH target as the account used by the MCP server. ssh_db_list is classified as read-only and remains available in readonly and restricted server security modes, so this path bypasses the command-execution boundary those modes are intended to enforce. The dump and import builders are blocked in readonly mode but remain vulnerable in the default unrestricted mode. The earlier version 3.6.5 hardening covered only ssh_db_query query text; it did not protect the list, dump, import, or restore builders, or the connection flags used by query builders. This issue is fixed in version 3.6.7.

RabbitMQ is a messaging and streaming broker. In the affected revision identified by the advisory, the AMQP 1.0 server_mode parser in deps/amqp10_common/src/amqp10_binary_parser.erl stops at the first body section and preserves the remaining bytes in bare_and_footer without validating message-section order. An authenticated publisher with write permission can place a properties section carrying a forged user-id after the body, causing rabbit_access_control:check_user_id/2 to see no user-id while permissive downstream AMQP 1.0 decoders or AMQP 0-9-1 conversion through classic and quorum queues expose the forged identity. Applications that rely on RabbitMQ-validated user-id metadata can therefore accept attacker-controlled publisher attribution. Strict consumers that reject out-of-order sections are not vulnerable to identity spoofing, and the issue does not bypass broker routing or destination authorization. This issue is fixed in version 4.3.5.
Improper input validation within the AmdPlatformRasSmm driver could allow an attacker with privileged access to overwrite SMRAM, potentially resulting in arbitrary code execution.

Insufficient Granularity of Access Control in AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) firmware could allow a malicious hypervisor to potentially redirect accesses to MMIO memory resulting in loss of guest memory integrity.
Improper address validation in the AMD RAID Configuration Driver could allow an attacker with administrative access to read arbitrary kernel memory, potentially resulting in loss of confidentiality.

Incomplete cleanup during VMRUN error handling could allow access to a Secure Encrypted Virtualization-Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) guest register state, potentially resulting in information disclosure and impacts to confidentiality.

Improper verification of a cryptographic signature in the PSP Boot ROM of AMD Zeppelin (Zen1/Zen+) processors could allow an attacker with local access to the SPI flash to bypass secure boot authentication, potentially resulting in arbitrary unsigned code execution at full Platform Security Processor privilege, loss of confidentiality, loss of integrity of the host boot chain, and persistent loss of availability.

Insufficient authorization in personal notification rules in Checkmk <2.5.0p20, <2.4.0p41 and 2.3.0 (EOL) allows authenticated users to receive notifications for hosts and services they are not a contact of by defining broad personal notification rules.

In iceoryx2 versions from 0.6.0 to 0.10.0, The C API getters that copy a service's hash into a caller-provided buffer (e.g. iox2_port_factory_pub_sub_service_hash and its other messaging protocol counterparts) write one byte past the end of the caller's buffer when `buffer_len` is less or equal to 40. The out-of-bounds byte is the string's NUL terminator, written at `buffer[buffer_len]`.



Resolution:



Resolution



The bugfix is released with iceoryx2 version 0.10.1 and on main branch (commit 7ca14dd).



Please note that the language bindings for C/C++ and Python (including the iceoryx2-ffi-c crate) are not published to crates.io since they are a local development dependency.

A privilege escalation vulnerability in the Axivion Suite ApiToken permission restriction for OIDC and SAML users of the Axivion Dashboard. 
When a user creates an ApiToken with a restricted token type (for example, IDE plugin or Continuous Integration), some of that user’s permissions should be removed from the token. For users who sign in to the Dashboard through OIDC, or through the SAML preview feature, this restriction has no effect. Exploitability is low: an attacker needs an ApiToken that has been leaked, or one that was shared on the assumption that its permissions were restricted.

Improper certificate validation vulnerability in Estonian Information System Authority (RIA) libdigidocpp, Estonian Information System Authority (RIA) DigiDoc4, Estonian Information System Authority (RIA) DigiDoc on Android, and Estonian Information System Authority (RIA) DigiDoc on iOS.


The vulnerability occurs because libdigidocpp does not properly validate
 the Extended Key Usage (EKU) extension of certificates used to sign 
OCSP responses. Specifically, it fails to verify that the certificate 
contains the id-kp-OCSPSigning EKU, which identifies certificates 
authorised to sign OCSP responses. 





This issue affects libdigidocpp: from 3.10.0 before 4.5.2; DigiDoc4: from 4.0.0 before 4.11.2; DigiDoc: from 3.0.0 before 3.2.0; DigiDoc: from 3.0.1 before 3.2.0.

An unauthenticated stored and reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the embedded web interface of Frontier Smart Technologies Venice X FS2340 running IR4.9 allows a network attacker with access to the interface to inject attacker-controlled JavaScript that may execute in the browser of a user accessing affected content.



Successful exploitation may allow the attacker to access information available within the browser's security context or perform actions through the affected web interface with the privileges of the affected user.



During authorized security testing, certain crafted JavaScript and code-injection payloads were also observed to cause the embedded web interface to crash and become temporarily unavailable on some tested software versions. This behavior represents a denial-of-service condition affecting the embedded web management interface; no device-level denial of service was established.

Synchronet BBS, in versions 3.20b to 3.21e, contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the answer() function when processing the terminal attribute of the SSH service. The call to cryptGetAttributeString() does not limit the copy to the size of the destination buffer, of which 41 bytes are used. An unauthenticated remote client can send a TERM value of up to 64 bytes and overwrite adjacent fields of the session object. If the SSH service is enabled, this tampering can cause connection threads to be blocked for an extended period, even after the client has disconnected. By exhausting the available sockets, the attacker can prevent new connections and cause a denial of service requiring the software to be restarted.

On Windows, the tarfile "tar" and "data" extraction filters did not reject member names or link targets that have a drive but no root, such as "C:foo". When extracting to a relative destination, such a member was written to the current working directory of that drive instead of the destination, and a symbolic link with such a target pointed outside the destination. The filters now refuse these member names and link targets with AbsolutePathError and AbsoluteLinkError.

In mcp-server-git before 2026.10.28, the --repository restriction can be bypassed through a nested directory that contains a .git file with a gitdir pointer to a repository outside the allowed path. A caller who can invoke the server's tools, place such a file in the allowed tree, and knows the outside repository's path can read committed content from that repository and create branches in it.

In mcp-server-fetch from 2026.10.10 and before 2026.11.11, the check that blocks requests to non-public addresses treats IPv6 site-local addresses (fec0::/10) as public. A fetch to such an address passes the server-side request forgery guard. Practical impact is limited because many hosts have no route to this range.

MISP contains an authorization bypass in the galaxy cluster detachment functionality. Users holding the sync role permission were incorrectly exempted from the tagger and organisation ownership checks when detaching galaxy clusters from events or attributes.

This allowed a sync user belonging to one organisation to remove galaxy cluster associations (threat intelligence tags) from events and attributes owned by a different organisation. The sync permission was intended for replication workflows, which never invoke the cluster detachment code path, but was erroneously used as a blanket authorization bypass.

Impact:
- Cross-organisation data integrity: a sync user can strip threat intelligence cluster associations from other organisations' events and attributes.
- Disruption of shared threat intelligence: removal of cluster tags can alter the analytical context of events visible to other users.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with the sync role permission (perm_sync) and tagger permission (perm_tagger).
- The target event or attribute must belong to a different organisation than the attacker.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP Collections retained a sharing group reference (sharing_group_id) even when the collection's distribution level was below 4 (i.e., not restricted to a sharing group). As a result, the sharing group name and UUID were displayed in the collection index and view endpoints to any user who could see the collection, regardless of whether that user was a member of the sharing group. Additionally, when collections were pushed to remote MISP servers, the sharing group data was included in the push payload even for collections not distributed to a sharing group, potentially leaking the group identity to remote systems.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with sufficient access to view the affected collection (e.g., a collection with distribution 0-3 that is publicly or broadly visible).
- The collection must have a stale sharing_group_id stored from a prior save.

Impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of the sharing group name and UUID to users outside the group.
- Potential leakage of sharing group structure to remote MISP servers via the push mechanism.
- An attacker could enumerate sharing group names to identify targeting opportunities.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP's interactive CLI shell, when used to edit or disable a user account, did not update the user record's modification timestamp. The application's session validation mechanism relies on this timestamp to detect that a user's record has changed and to reload the user's state in all active sessions.

As a result, a user who was disabled or had their role or permissions modified through the CLI would retain their existing authenticated session and continue to operate with their previous privileges until the session naturally expired. The administrative intent to revoke or reduce access was not enforced on already-active sessions.

Preconditions:
- An administrator performs a user edit or disable action via the MISP interactive CLI shell rather than the web interface.
- The target user has one or more active web sessions at the time of the change.

Impact:
- A disabled user retains full access to the MISP instance for the duration of their existing session.
- A user whose role or permissions were reduced via the CLI continues to operate with their prior, higher privileges in open sessions.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the feed and server event preview pages. When a remote MISP instance (configured as a feed source or connected server) supplies object or reference UUIDs and IDs containing special characters, these values are rendered in the preview HTML without proper escaping.

The vulnerable behavior occurs in two contexts:

- HTML element identifiers and text content: Remote UUIDs and IDs are inserted into DOM element IDs and visible text without HTML encoding, allowing injection of arbitrary HTML markup.
- Inline JavaScript event handlers: Remote UUIDs and IDs are embedded into onClick handler strings using only HTML escaping, which does not protect against JavaScript string-literal breakout. A crafted value containing a single quote can terminate the string and inject arbitrary JavaScript.

An attacker who controls a remote MISP instance (feed or server peer) can craft UUID or ID fields with a malicious payload. When an authenticated user on the victim instance views the corresponding event preview, the injected script executes in the user's browser within the MISP application origin, potentially allowing session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions on behalf of the user.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a stored cross-site script (XSS) vulnerability in the event review page used for merge, import, and enrichment workflows.

Object references displayed on this page include the UUID, name, and meta-category of the referenced object. These values originate from imported data (another event, a module result, or an import file) and were rendered into the HTML output without any encoding or sanitization.

An attacker who can supply or influence imported MISP-format data can embed arbitrary HTML or JavaScript in the referenced object's UUID, name, or meta-category fields. When a user views the review page, the malicious script executes in the user's browser context.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be able to introduce data into a MISP instance (e.g., via import, module enrichment, or event merge).
- A victim user must open the affected review page in a browser.

Security impact:
- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the MISP web application.
- Potential theft of session tokens, manipulation of user actions, or exfiltration of sensitive threat-intelligence data visible on the page.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in its map attachment rendering. When a GPX or GeoJSON file is uploaded as an attachment to a MISP event, the waypoint names (GPX) and property names and values (GeoJSON) are inserted into Leaflet map popups without HTML escaping. Because Leaflet renders popup content as raw HTML, any markup or script embedded in those fields is executed in the browser of every user who views the map and interacts with the affected marker or icon.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with permission to upload attachments to a MISP event crafts a GPX or GeoJSON file containing malicious HTML/JavaScript in waypoint names or GeoJSON property keys/values.
- A victim user views the event map and clicks the affected marker or GeoJSON icon, triggering the popup.

Impact:
- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the MISP web application, potentially leading to session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the event report element rendering pipeline. The client-side sanitization function used to prepare values for doT templates only escaped ampersand, less-than, and greater-than characters. However, the templates place these values inside double-quoted HTML attributes. Because double-quote and single-quote characters were not escaped, a user with the ability to author or modify report element values could inject a quote character to break out of the attribute context and inject arbitrary HTML or JavaScript that executes in the viewing user's browser.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be an authenticated user with permission to create or edit event report elements (e.g., a report author).
- A victim must open or view the crafted report in a browser.

Security impact:
- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the victim's MISP session.
- Potential theft of session tokens, sensitive data, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Overmind server preview's analyst data badge component. When rendering the analyst data link for a remote attribute, the remote server's UUID value was inserted into an inline JavaScript event handler using only HTML entity encoding, which is insufficient to prevent breakout from the JavaScript string context within the HTML attribute.

An attacker who can control or influence the UUID value of a remote attribute (for example, through a malicious or compromised upstream MISP server sharing data via Overmind) could inject arbitrary JavaScript that executes in the context of the victim's MISP session when the analyst data badge is clicked.

Preconditions:
- The victim must be authenticated to a MISP instance with Overmind enabled.
- The victim must view a remote event preview containing the crafted UUID.
- The victim must interact with (click) the analyst data badge element.

Security impact:
- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session.
- Potential theft of session credentials, manipulation of page content, or initiation of unauthorized actions on behalf of the authenticated user.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains an authorization flaw in the data capture and import paths for events, galaxies, galaxy clusters, analyst data, and sightings. A user who is neither a sync user nor a site admin could create or import records attributed to an organisation other than their own, or cause the creation of a new organisation from a payload-supplied identifier.

The root cause is an inconsistent authorization check: the code validated one representation of the creator organisation (for example a numeric ID or a UUID field) while storing a different representation taken directly from the user-supplied payload. In the event import path, a MISP export naming another organisation or a fabricated one was accepted and stored under that organisation. In the galaxy, cluster, analyst data, and sighting capture paths, the nested organisation object from the payload was used to create or reference an organisation without verifying the caller's membership.

Impact:
- Data (events, galaxies, clusters, analyst notes, sightings) can be created under an organisation the attacker does not belong to, polluting that organisation's data and potentially exposing it to that organisation's members.
- New organisations can be created from attacker-supplied identifiers, introducing phantom entities into the MISP instance.
- The integrity of the threat-intelligence data store is compromised because attribution is no longer trustworthy.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains an authorization bypass in its tag attachment functionality. The endpoints responsible for editing event tags, editing attribute tags, and adding tags to event reports accepted arbitrary tag IDs without verifying whether the authenticated user was permitted to attach the referenced tag.

The events/addTag endpoint already resolved tag IDs through a restricted lookup that enforced per-user and per-organisation tag visibility rules. However, the three tag-editor endpoints (editEventTags, editAttributeTags, and eventReports/addTag) passed the supplied tag IDs directly to the attachment logic without any such check.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with tagger and add permissions on the target event/attribute/report.
- Knowledge or discovery of a tag ID that is restricted (local_only) to another organisation.

Impact:
- A user can attach a tag that is restricted to a different organisation, effectively bypassing the tag visibility and scoping model.
- A local_only tag can be attached as a global tag, violating the intended distribution restriction and potentially exposing the existence or semantics of another organisation's restricted tag to a broader audience.
- Data integrity of the MISP instance is compromised as the tag association model no longer reflects the intended access-control boundaries.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the handling of Galaxy and Galaxy Cluster publish/unpublish operations. The application failed to enforce consistent permission checks when users attempted to unpublish a Galaxy or Galaxy Cluster. Specifically, the unpublish action only required the 'perm_galaxy_editor' permission, whereas the publish action required both 'perm_galaxy_editor' and 'perm_publish'.

This inconsistency allowed a user from a different organization who possessed the 'perm_galaxy_editor' permission but lacked the 'perm_publish' permission to unpublish a Galaxy or Galaxy Cluster created by another organization. This action could disrupt the availability of shared threat intelligence data for other users and organizations relying on that cluster.

The vulnerability affects MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains an authorization flaw in the Sharing Group Blueprint execution path. When a blueprint is executed, it rewrites the organisation roster of the associated sharing group. The check verifying that the blueprint's owning organisation still holds the right to extend (modify) that group was performed only once, at the time the blueprint was created. It was not re-evaluated at execution time.

As a result, an organisation that subsequently lost its extend permission or was entirely removed from the sharing group could still execute its existing blueprint and overwrite the group's organisation roster, adding or removing member organisations at will.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user belonging to an organisation that previously had extend rights on a sharing group
- A blueprint already exists in that group owned by the attacker's organisation
- The attacker's extend rights have been revoked or the organisation has been removed from the group after the blueprint was created

Security impact:
- Unauthorised modification of a sharing group's organisation roster
- Potential unauthorised addition of organisations to a sharing group, exposing shared indicators and events
- Bypass of the intended access-control model for sharing group membership

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52

MISP contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in the handling of sightings during server synchronization and bulk operations. The vulnerability allows a remote attacker with access to a synchronized MISP instance to pull sightings for events that are not shared with their organization or community. The sighting pull mechanism previously executed with elevated privileges and accepted event identifiers without verifying that the local event was authorized for sharing with the remote server. Additionally, the bulk save functionality for sightings did not strictly enforce that the attributes referenced in the request belonged to the specific event specified in the URL, allowing an attacker to associate sightings with unauthorized events by referencing attributes from other events. This can lead to unauthorized disclosure of threat intelligence data and integrity issues where sightings are incorrectly attributed to events the attacker should not access. 
The issue was reported by ENISA and fixed in version 2.5.52.

MISP trusted client-supplied forwarded IP headers (such as X-Forwarded-For) without verifying that the request originated from a known proxy or that the value was a valid IP address. The configured header value was accepted as the authoritative client IP for all security-relevant functions.

An unauthenticated remote attacker could forge the forwarded header to:
- Bypass IP-based restrictions on API authentication keys
- Evade brute-force / rate-limiting protection
- Inject arbitrary values into application and ECS logs, corrupting audit trails

The vulnerability required the MISP.log_client_ip_header setting to be configured to a forwarded header (e.g. HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR), which is a common deployment when MISP sits behind a reverse proxy.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52

MISP's LDAP authentication components (LdapAuth plugin and Apache LDAP authentication) unconditionally re-enabled user accounts that had been disabled by an administrator. During the user provisioning or update step of an LDAP login, the disabled flag was reset to enabled regardless of the account's current state.

This allowed any user with valid LDAP credentials to bypass an administrative disable action simply by authenticating, effectively nullifying the ability to revoke access through account deactivation.

- Affects the LdapAuth plugin and the ApacheSecureAuth component
- The insecure behavior was the default; no special configuration was required to trigger it
- An administrator's decision to disable a user (e.g., after a security incident or employee departure) could be reversed by the user's next successful LDAP login

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52

MISP's LinOTPAuth plugin, used for one-time-password authentication against a LinOTP server, did not enforce TLS server certificate verification when the LinOTPAuth.verifyssl configuration option was not explicitly set. In a default or minimally configured deployment, the authentication request to the LinOTP server was sent without peer or peer-name certificate validation, effectively allowing self-signed or spoofed certificates.

An attacker with a network position between the MISP instance and the LinOTP server could perform a man-in-the-middle attack to intercept or tamper with the authentication exchange, potentially capturing one-time passwords or user credentials.

Preconditions:
- The LinOTPAuth plugin is enabled and configured to communicate with a LinOTP server
- The LinOTPAuth.verifyssl setting is absent or null (not explicitly set to true or false)
- The attacker can position themselves on the network path between MISP and the LinOTP server

Security impact:
- Confidentiality of OTP tokens and authentication credentials in transit
- Potential for credential interception or replay

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52

MISP contains a vulnerability in its password reset (forgot password) functionality where the base URL used to construct the reset link sent by email could be derived from the HTTP request's Host header rather than from an explicitly configured value.

An unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request with a malicious Host header. If the application's base URL was not explicitly configured (MISP.baseurl or MISP.external_baseurl), the bootstrap would derive it from the request, and the resulting password reset email would contain a link pointing to the attacker-controlled domain. When the victim clicks the link, they are directed to the attacker's site, enabling credential phishing or token theft.

Preconditions:
- The password reset feature (allow_password_forgotten) is enabled
- MISP.baseurl and MISP.external_baseurl are not explicitly set to trusted values
- The victim initiates or is targeted for a password reset

Impact:
- Phishing: victim is redirected to an attacker-controlled URL instead of the legitimate MISP instance
- Potential credential compromise if the victim enters credentials on the attacker's site
- No direct compromise of the MISP server itself

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52

MISP accepted compressed HTTP request bodies (gzip, brotli, zstd) and decompressed them before authentication was performed, with no limit on the size of the resulting decompressed data. An unauthenticated attacker could send a small compressed payload that expands to a very large decompressed body, exhausting server memory and causing a denial of service. Brotli and zstd, with their high compression ratios, made the attack particularly effective.

The vulnerability required no authentication and no special conditions beyond the ability to send an HTTP request with a Content-Encoding header. The impact is a complete loss of availability for the affected MISP instance.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a denial-of-service vulnerability in its image processing pipeline. When generating attachment thumbnails or rendering event graph preview images, the application decodes user-supplied image data using the GD library without first validating the declared pixel dimensions in the image header.

Because GD allocates its pixel buffers outside the scope of PHP's memory_limit directive, a crafted image with an extremely large declared resolution (for example, 20000 x 20000 pixels) can trigger a multi-gigabyte memory allocation during the decode step, exhausting available system memory and causing the PHP worker process or the host to become unresponsive.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated MISP user with permission to upload attachments or to create/view event graphs.
- The ability to supply a crafted image file (e.g., a PNG with a valid header declaring oversized dimensions).

Impact:
- Denial of service: memory exhaustion leading to process crash or host unavailability.
- No confidentiality or integrity impact is indicated by the evidence.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its feed and sync HTTP request handling. When the application uses libcurl as the HTTP transport, the CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION option was enabled by default, causing the library to automatically follow HTTP redirects without the application's own per-hop validation logic being invoked.

- Feed requests: MISP implements its own redirect validation for feed sources, but libcurl was following redirects before that validation could execute, allowing a malicious or compromised feed source to redirect the request to arbitrary internal URLs.
- Sync requests: Sync peers are server-configured, and the application does not perform per-hop redirect validation for sync traffic. libcurl's automatic redirect following allowed a malicious sync peer to redirect the request to internal network resources.

An attacker who is a configured sync peer, controls a feed source URL, or can influence DNS resolution for a configured endpoint can exploit this to cause the MISP server to issue requests to arbitrary internal services, potentially reading sensitive data or interacting with internal APIs that are not otherwise exposed.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP's NIDS rule export functionality for Snort and Suricata formats does not properly escape user-controlled data before embedding it into generated rule text. Attribute values, tag names, and URL paths are inserted directly into rule options (msg, metadata, content matches) without neutralizing characters that are syntactically significant in the NIDS rule grammar, such as double quotes, semicolons, backslashes, commas, and control characters.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify attributes in a MISP instance can craft attribute values or tag names containing these special characters. When the NIDS rules are exported, the unescaped data breaks out of the intended option or content field, allowing injection of arbitrary rule options, corruption of rule structure, or generation of syntactically invalid rules that may cause the downstream NIDS engine to reject the entire ruleset.

The affected export paths include:
- Snort and Suricata msg: option (quotes, semicolons, backslashes, control characters)
- Suricata metadata: option (commas, semicolons, quotes, whitespace, control characters)
- Suricata http.uri content: match for URL path (quotes, semicolons, pipe characters)

Security impact is limited to the integrity and availability of the exported NIDS rules and the downstream NIDS engine that consumes them. There is no direct compromise of the MISP application itself.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) in its correlation management functionality.

The top-correlation cache regeneration and occurrence count regeneration actions were accessible via bodyless GET requests and were triggered from the admin interface using plain hyperlinks rather than POST forms. Because these state-changing operations did not require a POST method and were reachable through simple URL navigation, an attacker who can induce an authenticated administrator to visit a malicious page or click a crafted link can trigger these operations without the administrator's explicit consent.

Impact:
- Unintended triggering of resource-intensive correlation regeneration processes
- Potential disruption of correlation data processing and increased server load
- No direct data disclosure or corruption is evidenced

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52

MISP contains a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) vulnerability in its Warninglist feature. Warninglist entries of type "regex" are evaluated against attribute values without any backtracking limit. An authenticated user with permission to add or import warninglist entries can supply a crafted regular expression pattern that triggers excessive backtracking in the PCRE engine, causing sustained CPU consumption and denial of service.

Additionally, imported warninglists were not validated for syntactic correctness before replacing existing entries, allowing malformed or malicious patterns to be persisted and later evaluated without prior rejection.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated account with the ability to create, edit, or import warninglist entries (users below site-admin level can add entries).
- The target MISP instance has at least one warninglist of type "regex" that will be evaluated against incoming attribute values.

Impact:
- Sustained CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service for all users of the MISP instance.
- Potential for cascading performance degradation on shared infrastructure.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains an improper output sanitization vulnerability in the Zeek (Bro) intelligence export functionality.

The export module constructs tab-separated lines for downstream Zeek/Bro intelligence feeds. The sanitization routine was intended to strip tab, newline, and carriage-return characters from user-controlled fields (organisation names and attribute values) before they were embedded into the export line format. However, the sanitization pipeline applied character replacement before HTML entity decoding, meaning that HTML entities such as 	 (tab), 
 (newline), and  (carriage return) survived the initial pass and were subsequently decoded into actual separator characters. Additionally, organisation names were inserted into the export format string without any sanitization at all.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify events, organisation names, or attribute values could embed HTML-encoded separator characters. When the Zeek/Bro export was generated, these characters would split a single export line into multiple lines or introduce extra tab-delimited fields, corrupting the structured intelligence feed consumed by downstream Zeek/Bro deployments.

Security impact:
- Integrity of exported intelligence data is compromised; downstream Zeek/Bro systems may process malformed or split entries.
- Corrupted intelligence lines could lead to incorrect blocking, alerting, or logging decisions in the consuming environment.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains multiple related authorization and input-validation flaws in its object editing and attachment handling workflows.

- A user with permission to edit their own object could inject a foreign attribute identifier into the object revision form. The revision data, stored in the server-side session, was merged into the stored object before the save diff was computed. The save then wrote to the foreign attribute row by its identifier without verifying that the row belonged to the caller's event or organisation, allowing an attacker to overwrite or soft-delete an attribute in another organisation's private event.
- Attachment file paths were constructed directly from event and attribute identifiers supplied by the request. Because no type or format validation was applied, crafted values (for example directory-traversal sequences or file-name extensions) could cause the application to read from or write to file-system locations outside the intended attachment directory.
- The audit-log behaviour recorded an edit under the event identifier carried in the save payload rather than the event identifier of the stored database row. An attacker who included a different event identifier in the save could cause the audit entry to be attributed to the wrong event, undermining the integrity of the audit trail.

Exploitation requires an authenticated web-session user with object-editing permissions (perm_add / perm_modify). API-key-only requests do not carry the PHP session and are not affected by the revision-session vector.

Affected versions: MISP < 2.5.52. Fixed in 2.5.52.

MISP contains a type confusion vulnerability in the authentication key creation endpoint. When a user submits a floating-point value as the target user identifier, the authorization check truncates the value to an integer (matching the attacker's own account), while the persistence layer rounds the same value to a different integer (the next account in the sequence). This discrepancy allows an authenticated user with key-creation permission to generate an API authentication key belonging to another user.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be an authenticated user with the permission to create authentication keys.
- The target user must have a consecutive numeric identifier immediately following the attacker's identifier.

Impact:
- Unauthorized creation of an API key for another user, granting the attacker access to that user's data and operations within the MISP instance.
- The vulnerability is trivially exploitable by substituting a carefully crafted floating-point value for the integer user identifier in the request.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains multiple flaws in its login and one-time-password (OTP) brute-force lockout mechanism that collectively weaken authentication protection.

- Lockout counter bypass: the lockout stored and matched usernames using a single-byte case-fold function. An email address containing a non-ASCII capital letter (for example a Latin-1 or Cyrillic uppercase) was never counted toward the lockout threshold, allowing unlimited failed login attempts against that account.
- Collation-folding authentication bypass: the database collation performs accent and width folding, so a Unicode variant of a valid address (e.g. a different diacritic or a full-width character) resolved to the same account during authentication while the lockout treated it as a distinct, untracked identity. An attacker could therefore authenticate as the target user using a folded alias without triggering the lockout.
- Username enumeration via NUL byte: submitting a password containing a NUL byte caused the hashing routine to raise an exception, producing an HTTP 500 response for a known account but a different response for an unknown one, disclosing valid usernames.

Preconditions: the target MISP instance is reachable over the network and the login endpoint is exposed. No prior authentication is required.

Security impact: an unauthenticated attacker can perform unlimited password-guessing against accounts whose address contains a non-ASCII capital, can authenticate as a user via a Unicode-folded alias, and can enumerate valid usernames. Successful exploitation leads to account takeover.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

MISP's brute-force lockout mechanism for login and one-time-password (OTP) authentication is susceptible to bypass through Unicode case-folding inconsistencies and input handling flaws.

- Email addresses containing non-ASCII capital letters are not counted toward the lockout threshold, permitting unlimited authentication attempts against a specific account.
- Database collation folding (accent and width variants) allows an attacker to reach a valid account using a folded alias of the email address without the attempt being recorded in the lockout counter.
- A password containing a NUL byte produces a distinct server error for known accounts while unknown accounts receive a different response, enabling username enumeration.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit these issues to perform unlimited password brute-force attacks against any account and to enumerate valid user accounts.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52

MISP contains a DOM-based cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Pivot Explorer component. The bundled pivotick visualization library (version 1.2.0) rendered all string values it received as HTML markup rather than as plain text. As a result, user-controllable data fields, including attribute comments, attribute values, and reference relationship types, were interpreted and executed as HTML/JavaScript in the Pivot Explorer tooltip and sidebar panels.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify MISP attributes could embed malicious HTML or script payloads in these fields. When another user (or the same user) opened the Pivot Explorer and viewed the affected event data, the injected markup would execute in the victim's browser context, potentially allowing session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must have authenticated access to create or modify MISP attributes (comments, values, or reference relationship types).
- The victim must open the Pivot Explorer and interact with or view the affected event data in the tooltip or sidebar.

Security impact: Successful exploitation allows arbitrary script execution in the victim's browser within the MISP application origin, enabling theft of session credentials, manipulation of displayed data, and execution of privileged API calls on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

A potential security vulnerability has been identified in the HP Hotkey UWP Service, which might allow escalation of privilege. HP is releasing mitigation for the potential vulnerability. Customers using HP Programmable Key are recommended to update HP Hotkey Support.

Lookyloo is a web-based URL capture and analysis platform. Prior to the fix, the authorization mechanism for private captures (seed-based access control) was not consistently enforced at the data access layer. The capture_cache method and numerous internal methods (get_info, get_meta, get_statistics, get_modules_responses, get_data, get_video, get_screenshot, get_har, get_cookies, get_storage_state, get_frames, get_console_messages, get_capture, get_ressource, misp_export, lacus_export, ai_export, comparator functions, and others) could be invoked with only a capture UUID without validating the required seed token. This meant that API endpoints and internal code paths that called these methods directly could return private capture data to unauthenticated users or users lacking the correct seed. The before_request hook in the web interface provided a partial check, but the underlying data layer did not enforce it, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary. An attacker who knew or guessed a private capture UUID could potentially access sensitive data including rendered screenshots, HAR files, downloaded files, cookies, storage state, console messages, and MISP exports through various REST API endpoints and web routes. The fix introduces a LookylooPrivateCapture exception raised at the cache layer when a private capture is accessed without a valid seed, refactors the API to pass CaptureCache objects (already validated) rather than raw UUIDs, and ensures all web and API endpoints propagate the session-known seed or admin status to the data access layer. Background processes use an explicit unsafe=True flag to bypass the check, as they operate server-side with full trust.

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. In versions prior to 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9 and 19.3.1, react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-parcel, and react-server-dom-turbopack are vulnerable to denial of service. Specially crafted HTTP requests sent to server function endpoints can cause out-of-memory exceptions or excessive CPU usage. This issue is fixed in versions 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9 and 19.3.1.

SQL injection in WHMCS could allow an authenticated client with View & Manage Contacts permission to retrieve other clients' personal, billing, and support information, as well as administrator account records and password hashes.
SQL injection in WHMCS could allow an unauthenticated user to retrieve clients' personal and support information, as well as administrator account records and password hashes.

Pelican 4.12.0 contains an OS command injection vulnerability in pelican-import. An attacker-controlled wp:post_name from a WordPress XML export is used in an output filename that is interpolated into a Pandoc command passed to subprocess.call with shell=True. On POSIX systems, command substitution in the slug is evaluated when a user imports the crafted export.

n8n is an open source workflow automation platform. Prior to 1.123.90 and 2.14.0, the invitation acceptance endpoint accepts inviter and invitee user IDs without a signed invitation token, allowing any preexisting member to take over a pending new user account. A member with permission to list users can read the ID of a pending account and set its password without authentication, then log in as that user, including as an admin when the invitation has the admin role. Exploitation requires an invitation that has not been accepted yet. This issue is fixed in versions 1.123.90 and 2.14.0.

n8n is an open source workflow automation platform. Prior to 2.47.6, 2.48.3, and 3.2.2, the password reset link and role change operations do not protect the instance owner account from users with a custom instance role. A user whose custom instance role includes user management permissions can obtain a password reset link for the owner and take over the owner account, or change the owner's role, gaining full control of the instance. Exploitation requires the custom roles feature and a custom instance role with user management permissions. This issue is fixed in versions 2.47.6, 2.48.3, and 3.2.2.

An information disclosure vulnerability in Zstandard versions 1.5.1 through 1.5.7 allows specially crafted compressed data to expose the contents of an internal buffer through decompressed output. The buffer is 64 KiB in the default configuration and may contain uninitialized memory or literals from earlier decompressions performed using the same decompression context. An attacker who can submit compressed data and observe the resulting output can recover the buffer's contents.

An Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command（'OS Command Injection') in the ASUS GPU Tweak III allows a remote user to execute arbitrary OS commands via a crafted request to an HTTP endpoint of the service.
Refer to the '
Security Update for ASUS GPU Tweak III  ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization and Use After Free in certain ASUS router models allows an unauthenticated nearby user to cause the service to write unexpected values or crash the system under specific timing conditions.
Refer to the ' Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

Out-of-bounds write vulnerability in certain ASUS routers allows an unauthenticated nearby user to corrupt process memory, potentially resulting in a denial-of-service, via crafted LLTD packets.Refer to the ' Security Update for ASUS Router Firmware ' section on the ASUS Security Advisory for more information.

Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code or inject SQL through a forged keyset pagination cursor.

Ash.Page.Keyset.filter/4 in lib/ash/page/keyset.ex decodes the client-supplied page[:after] or page[:before] cursor from Erlang external term format and rejects decoded expressions with Ash.Expr.expr?/1. That check does not examine the fields of a struct. The cast of each value against the type of its sort field accepts structs for the :ci_string, :map, :struct and :term types. A struct in the cursor value for such a sort field therefore reaches the data layer. With AshPostgres, the read passes such a struct to inspect/1, which runs the Inspect implementation of the struct module that the attacker selected. A chain of struct modules from ecto and db_connection then calls a function that the cursor names, which permits OS command execution. An %Ash.Query.Function.Fragment{} inside an %Ash.CiString{} value is written into the SQL query as raw text.

This issue affects ash: from 3.31.3 before 3.38.0.
Any WiFi client can send HTTP DELETE to /meeting-recording/delete to permanently delete files without authentication.
Endpoints accessible without authentication from any WiFi client (e.g., /user/hasSimCard, /user/pooling, /api/device-info).

The Foxtool All-in-One: Contact chat button, Custom login, Media optimize images WordPress plugin through 2.5.4 does not check that the current user owns or may delete a post's featured image before permanently deleting it along with the post, allowing users with a role as low as Contributor to delete arbitrary image attachments from the media library, such as those uploaded by administrators, when the option to delete attached images on post deletion is enabled.

The 3D Website Builder WordPress plugin through 2.0.3 does not perform any authorisation check in one of its publicly accessible AJAX actions, and the nonce guarding it is exposed to visitors on any page embedding the 3D Website Builder WordPress plugin through 2.0.3's shortcode, allowing unauthenticated users to permanently delete any of the 3D Website Builder WordPress plugin through 2.0.3's 3D builder objects and their slides.
Accessible without authentication via /user/resetPasswordFlagTest, forcing a password change prompt on the next admin login.
Admin password stored in plaintext at /data/data/com.acer.android.m3.webserver/shared_prefs/userInfo.xml, allowing any app with root or file access to read credentials directly.
After authentication, /user/getNetworkStatus discloses SIM phone number, cell tower ID (enabling geolocation), and network type.

System service 'antaiuiserver' exposes transaction 14 (sendMyATCmd) & 4, allowing ANY app on device to send arbitrary AT commands to modem without permissions (no READ_PHONE_STATE, SEND_SMS). Enables reading IMEI, IMSI, ICCID, and managing SMS.

Web administration panel (port 8080) binds to all network interfaces including public IPv6 addresses, making internal API endpoints reachable over WAN without firewall protection (related to CVE-2026-50224).
Any connected WiFi client can fetch device info and meeting recording metadata without credentials.

A format string vulnerability has been reported in the Internal Backup of ADM. User-controlled input from the source_folders parameter is passed by internalbackup.cgi to a shared string-copy routine in libbackup.so.0.0 and used directly as the format-string argument to snprintf() without corresponding variadic arguments. This may allow an authenticated attacker to disclose process memory addresses or trigger unintended memory writes that terminate the affected CGI process.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An externally-controlled format string vulnerability exists in the authenticated upload_wireguard action of settings/vpnupload.cgi in the ADM. The CGI takes an attacker-controlled WireGuard profile name, inserts it into a JSON object, serializes it, and passes the resulting formatted string directly to printf as the format argument without validation or escaping. An authenticated remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by sending format string specifiers, or leverage variadic read/write primitives within the non-PIE, non-Canary root CGI to potentially achieve arbitrary remote code execution with root privileges.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An externally controlled format string vulnerability in the Snapshot CGI components of ADM allows an authenticated administrator to cause repeatable premature termination of affected privileged CGI requests by supplying crafted input.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

Binding to an unrestricted IP address in the netstack SOCKS5 proxy of the NetBird client (client/iface/netstack) in NetBird versions before 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated attacker on the same network as the client to relay traffic through the client into its NetBird overlay network. When the client runs in netstack mode (NB_USE_NETSTACK_MODE=true), it starts a SOCKS5 proxy, without authentication, that is meant to bridge applications on the local host into the userspace WireGuard stack. The listener was bound to 0.0.0.0 instead of the loopback address, so any host that can reach the proxy port (1080 by default) can connect and reach peers and internal resources with the network position of the affected client. Netstack mode is not enabled by default. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, which binds the proxy to 127.0.0.1 by default.

Deserialization of untrusted data in the relay server handshake of NetBird versions 0.29.0 through 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to reach the Go encoding/gob decoder with attacker-supplied bytes before any credential is checked, which can lead to denial of service of the relay server. The deprecated Hello handshake message was still accepted before authentication and its token was decoded with gob.NewDecoder (shared/relay/auth/hmac) before the HMAC signature was verified. The handshake buffer limits the input to 212 bytes and the pre-authentication phase to 10 seconds, so there is no impact on confidentiality or integrity and the impact on availability depends on a separate weakness in the gob decoder of the Go toolchain used to build the relay server, such as CVE-2024-34156. The Auth handshake, used by clients since version 0.29.1, does not use gob. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which removes the Hello handshake and the gob-based token decoding.

A protection mechanism failure in the userspace firewall of the NetBird client (client/firewall/uspfilter) in NetBird versions 0.55.0 through 0.74.6 allows an attacker who controls an enrolled peer to bypass the access control rules of another peer by sending IP-fragmented packets. The packet filter returned an allow verdict for any IPv4 fragment, and for any IPv6 packet carrying a Fragment extension header, before evaluating the ACL rules. This applied to the leading fragment as well as to continuation fragments, so no part of a fragmented datagram was filtered and ports denied by policy could be reached. The userspace filter is the packet filter wherever the client does not program the kernel firewall, which includes the Android and iOS apps. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, in the Android app from version 0.6.0 and in the iOS app from version 0.3.3, which evaluate fragments against the same ACL rules as unfragmented packets.

An External Control of File Name or Path (Argument Injection) vulnerability in the settings/notification.cgi component of ADM allows authenticated remote administrators to create or truncate arbitrary files with root privileges via crafted request parameters. An authenticated administrator can truncate arbitrary critical files across the root filesystem, leading to system failure or Denial of Service (DoS).
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An argument injection vulnerability exists in the settings/vpn.cgi endpoint in the ADM. When processing a WireGuard profile, the internal command parser removes quotes and performs a quote-agnostic scan on arguments without properly sanitizing redirection operators. An authenticated administrator can supply a crafted parameter to cause the execution helper to open and truncate arbitrary files on the filesystem with root privileges, resulting in an arbitrary file truncation and denial-of-service (DoS) condition.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An arbitrary file creation and truncation vulnerability exists in the File Explorer of ADM. An authenticated low-privileged user can upload a file with crafted path components containing quote and redirection characters. When music.cgi processes the entry for audio playback operations, the unescaped path string breaks out of the expected argument context in the internal command parser. This causes the system execution helper to open the attacker-specified path with root privileges using O_TRUNC, allowing remote attackers to truncate or create arbitrary system files.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

A stack-based buffer overflow in the DHCP Server helper of ASUSTOR ADM allows an unauthenticated attacker on the local network to trigger stack memory corruption by sending a crafted DHCP hostname to a device with DHCP Server enabled. This may disrupt DHCP service.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

A potential stack-based buffer overflow exists in ADM Defender Firewall configuration handling. Before the fix, firewall policy processing used string operations without sufficient destination-size checks and did not consistently validate array bounds. Malformed or oversized configuration data may cause an out-of-bounds write and corrupt stack memory.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An OS command injection vulnerability in the PPPoE configuration of ADM allows an authenticated administrator to store shell syntax in the PPPoE account value. When the service loads the resulting configuration, the injected commands can execute with root privileges.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An improper input validation vulnerability in the OpenVPN client configuration import feature of ADM allows authenticated administrative users to execute arbitrary operating system commands via a crafted .ovpn profile.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

Reliance on an untrusted source of the client address in the WebSocket listener of the NetBird relay server (relay/server/listener/ws) in NetBird versions 0.31.1 through 0.74.7 allows an attacker with an enrolled peer to spoof the source address of their relay connection. The listener used the values of the X-Real-Ip and X-Real-Port request headers as the remote address of the connection unconditionally, without checking that the request came from a trusted upstream proxy. A WebSocket client that sends both headers makes the relay record and use an arbitrary address for its connection, including in the relay connection log, so a client can hide its real address or attribute its connection to another host. Only the relay server is affected; the NetBird client, including the Android and iOS apps, does not run the relay listener. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which honours these headers only for requests whose direct connection address is in a configured set of trusted proxies and ignores them by default.

A cleartext transmission of sensitive information vulnerability in the ADM Notifications allows network eavesdroppers on the outbound network path to obtain Clickatell service credentials via the SMS. When executing an SMS test for Clickatell Communicator Central, the backend function Send_Test_SMS embeds the sensitive contents directly into an unencrypted HTTP request URL. An observer on the NAS network egress path can capture the plain text credentials and message payload since the initial request is transmitted without TLS protection or secret redaction.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An improper certificate validation vulnerability exists in ADM App Central, due to disabled peer verification within the set-used-server endpoint, enabling an unauthenticated Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacker to intercept HTTPS traffic, bypass TLS validation, and modify App Central server redirection settings to cause a persistent service outage for application updates without bypassing package signature verification.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

A path traversal vulnerability in the regional options of ADM allows attackers to read arbitrary files on the system. The function fails to properly canonicalize user-supplied directory paths, enabling attackers to bypass path restriction checks via crafted path traversal sequences.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An improper TLS certificate validation vulnerability exists in the ADM online update service. An unauthenticated attacker capable of performing a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack against the device's firmware update connection can impersonate the update server using an untrusted TLS certificate and supply malicious update metadata. The attacker may cause a crafted firmware image to be installed and execute arbitrary code with root privileges when automatic firmware updates are enabled.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.
